summary: This memo proposes a protocol that, given a TCP port pair, returns a string naming the owner of that connection on the server's system. Suggested uses include identifying users during FTP sessions. It was replaced by RFC 931.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 912 proposes a service that answers who owns a TCP connection on the server's system. A client sends a pair of port numbers and receives a user identifier or an error response.

subtitle: A proposed TCP service that identifies the owner of a connection on the server system.

tldr.problem: Applications needed a way to ask a host which user owned a specified TCP connection on that host.
tldr.mechanism: The proposed server listens on TCP port 113, receives a pair of port numbers, and returns a system-dependent user identifier or an error.
tldr.outcome: RFC 912 is an informational proposal and was obsoleted by RFC 931.

today: RFC 912 is a proposed Authentication Service protocol and was obsoleted by RFC 931.

sections.title: Purpose and Connection Rules
sections.content:
The Authentication Server is intended to identify the owner of a particular TCP connection on the server's system. Suggested uses include identifying a user during FTP and checking a user for network file-server access.

The service listens on TCP port 113. Queries are allowed only for fully specified connections: a user on Host A can ask Host B about connections between A and B, using the query connection to supply the host pair.
sections.plainLanguage: A client asks the server who owns one of its TCP connections. The query can cover a connection between the client host and the server host.

sections.title: Queries and Responses
sections.content:
The client sends one text line containing the local and foreign TCP ports, separated by a comma. The local port is on the target server system; the foreign port is on the source user system. For example, the RFC shows 23, 6191.

The server responds with the same port pair, a response type, and additional information. USERID returns a printable identifier whose format is system-dependent. ERROR can include INVALID PORT, NO USER, or UNKNOWN ERROR. The server closes the connection after responding.
sections.plainLanguage: Send the two port numbers in a text line. The server returns a user identifier or an error explaining why it could not determine one.

sections.title: Trust in the Response
sections.content:
The RFC warns that authentication servers may differ in trustworthiness. Applications must decide how much trust to place in the returned information. It says that, in some cases, use may appropriately be restricted to a locally controlled subnet.

The memo lists automatic user authentication for FTP and verification for privileged network operations as possible applications. It does not itself make the returned identity trustworthy.
sections.plainLanguage: A returned name is only as reliable as the server that supplies it. Applications must decide whether to trust that server before using the answer.
